method: Each record pairs a public promise with the vote, signed bill, or official action on the same issue. Status reflects only the cited evidence. Nonpartisan; no vote recommendations.

said.text: In his 2025 State of the State address he named school choice an emergency item for the 89th Legislature and said it must pass that session.

did.text: Signed Senate Bill 2, which creates an education savings account program with about $1 billion in initial funding.

promises.rationale: The legislation he called an emergency item was passed and signed in the same session.

said.text: Named bail reform an emergency item and called for a constitutional amendment so judges could deny bail to defendants charged with the most serious violent crimes.

did.text: Signed SB 9, SB 40, HB 75 and SJR 5 on June 3, 2025. Voters approved SJR 5 as Proposition 3 on Nov 4, 2025, which lets judges deny bail for certain violent or sexual felonies.

promises.rationale: The bail package he prioritized was signed, and voters ratified the constitutional amendment.

said.text: Listed Senate Bill 4, which raises the school homestead exemption to $140,000 ($150,000 for seniors), among his top priority bills for the 2025 session.

did.text: The Legislature passed the increase. Voters approved Proposition 13, which raises the school homestead exemption from $100,000 to $140,000.

promises.rationale: The exemption level he prioritized became law after voter approval.

said.text: Listed Senate Bill 3, banning THC products in Texas, among his top 2025 priority bills.

did.text: SB 3 passed the Legislature but Gov. Abbott vetoed it, citing likely constitutional challenges. Abbott later issued Executive Order GA-56, which restricts sales to people 21 and older instead of banning them.

promises.rationale: The ban he championed passed the Senate but did not become law because of the governor's veto.

said.text: In a May 2025 interview he opposed the Republican reconciliation bill and disputed its description of Medicaid changes as reforms.

did.text: Voted No on final House passage of H.R. 1 (Roll Call 190). It passed 218-214.

promises.rationale: His recorded vote matches his stated opposition.

said.text: Stated opposition to the bill, saying it would cut health coverage and food aid and add to the national debt.

did.text: Voted No on final House passage of H.R. 1 (Roll Call 190). It passed 218-214.

promises.rationale: His recorded vote matches his stated position.

promises.issue: Legal challenges to federal administration actions

said.text: After the 2024 election he said his office had prepared for months and would take legal action if the incoming administration broke the law.

did.text: His office announced its 100th lawsuit against the administration in under two years, leading or co-leading 67 of them.

promises.rationale: He filed the litigation he said he would. Whether each suit succeeds is a separate question.

said.text: Declined a US Justice Department request for California's full, unredacted voter registration list, citing state laws that protect voters' data.

did.text: A federal judge dismissed the DOJ lawsuit seeking data on 23 million voters, and the full list was not turned over.

promises.rationale: The data she refused to release was not released, and a court upheld that outcome.

said.text: Said the state's chronically late annual financial report was being brought closer to on time and that the next report would be about two months late.

did.text: The FY 2024-25 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report was published in May 2026, after the March 31 target.

promises.rationale: The report came out about as she projected and much sooner than past years, but still after the target date.
